column1: Dynamic Data Masking obscures column values in {{c1::query results}}, not in the stored data.
column2:
DDM replaces sensitive values in the results returned to readers without UNMASK permission. For example, a query can return a masked email instead of its full address. The stored value does not change.
Review source

column1: For a masked reader, default() displays {{c1::xxxx}} for a non-NULL varchar(20) value.
column2:
The default string mask returns four lowercase x characters for a varchar(20) column. The replacement is fixed rather than based on the original text. A declared string length below four reduces the number of x characters.
Review source

column1: For a masked reader, default() replaces a non-NULL numeric value with {{c1::0}}.
column2:
A masked number is replaced by zero regardless of its original value. For example, a stored salary of 85000 displays as 0. Do not interpret that displayed zero as the actual salary.
Review source

column1: For a masked reader, default() displays {{c1::1900-01-01}} for a non-NULL date value.
column2:
The default date mask displays the fixed date 1900-01-01. It does not preserve the person's actual birth date or its year. The original date remains in the table.
Review source

column1: The email() mask keeps the first character but always uses the suffix {{c1::.com}}.
column2:
The mask keeps the first character, a, and replaces the rest with XXX@XXXX.com. The .com ending is fixed even when the real address ends in .net. The displayed address is not a real contact address.
Review source

column1: Use FUNCTION = '{{c1::random}}(10000, 100000)' to replace numeric values with random values in that range.
column2:
The low and high arguments define the replacement range, not a calculation from the stored value. For example, random(1, 12) displays a number in that range. Random choices can repeat, and they do not preserve the original data's meaning.
Review source

column1: To show no leading characters and retain the last four, use partial({{c1::0}}, "XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-", 4).
column2:
The first argument is the number of original characters to keep at the start. A value of 0 keeps none. The final argument, 4, preserves the last four characters after the replacement text.
Review source

column1: To retain the last four characters, use partial(0, "XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-", {{c1::4}}).
column2:
The third argument is the number of original characters to keep at the end. A value of 4 preserves the last four characters. The first argument, 0, keeps no original characters at the start.
Review source

column1: In the partial() mask, the {{c1::second argument}} specifies replacement text between the visible ends.
column2:
prefix and suffix are counts of original characters to keep at the start and end. padding is literal replacement text between them. For example, partial(1, "***", 2) turns ABCDE into A***DE.
Review source

column1: A masked email column can be defined as Email varchar(100) {{c1::MASKED WITH}} (FUNCTION = 'email()').
column2:
MASKED WITH attaches a masking function to a column definition. For example, Email varchar(100) MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = 'email()') applies the email mask. Readers still need SELECT, and readers with UNMASK can see the original value.
Review source

column1: Add a mask with ALTER TABLE dbo.Customers ALTER COLUMN DateOfBirth {{c1::ADD MASKED}} WITH (FUNCTION = 'default()');
column2:
ALTER TABLE identifies the table, and ALTER COLUMN identifies the existing column. ADD MASKED attaches the default masking rule without replacing stored dates. The reader's permissions determine whether query results display the mask.
Review source

column1: Remove a mask with ALTER TABLE dbo.Customers ALTER COLUMN DateOfBirth {{c1::DROP MASKED}};
column2:
DROP MASKED removes the display rule from the existing column. It does not delete the column or restore data from a backup because the stored values never changed. Readers can then see the original values through their normal read access.
Review source

column1: A reader needs {{c1::UNMASK}} to see actual values in dynamically masked columns.
column2:
UNMASK allows original values to appear instead of replacements. It does not give the user permission to query the table. The user also needs SELECT on the requested data.
Review source

column1: UNMASK alone is insufficient to retrieve data because the reader also needs {{c1::SELECT}}.
column2:
SELECT grants the right to read data, while UNMASK controls whether those results show the original sensitive values. A user with only UNMASK cannot query a table without read permission. These permissions solve separate access questions.
Review source

column1: Changing a mask on an existing column requires {{c1::ALTER ANY MASK}} plus ALTER on the table.
column2:
ALTER on the table permits table changes, while ALTER ANY MASK permits mask changes. The documented requirement combines both permissions. SELECT access alone does not authorize adding or removing a mask.
Review source

column1: Database {{c1::CONTROL}} permission includes UNMASK, so DDM does not hide plaintext from these administrators.
column2:
CONTROL includes UNMASK, so users with this broad permission can see original values. Database owners and sysadmin members are not suitable accounts for testing restricted masking behavior. DDM is not protection against these administrators.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2022+, grant schema-wide unmasking with GRANT UNMASK ON {{c1::SCHEMA}}::Sales TO SalesManager;
column2:
SCHEMA::Sales scopes UNMASK to the Sales schema. It does not grant SELECT or unmask objects in other schemas. This is useful when a role needs original values across a department's tables.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2022+, GRANT UNMASK ON dbo.Customers{{c1::(Phone)}} TO TelemarketingTeam; limits the grant to Phone.
column2:
The parentheses identify Phone as the only column covered by this UNMASK grant. Other masked columns in dbo.Customers remain subject to their own permissions. The role also needs SELECT on the data it reads.
Review source

column1: Schema-, table-, and column-level UNMASK grants became available in SQL Server {{c1::2022 (16.x)}}.
column2:
SQL Server 2022 added more specific UNMASK scopes. A role can unmask one column without unmasking every sensitive column it can read. Keep the product version in mind when studying this syntax.
Review source

column1: Add an existing user to an existing role with ALTER ROLE MaskedDataViewers {{c1::ADD MEMBER}} SupportStaff;
column2:
ALTER ROLE changes an existing role's membership. ADD MEMBER names the existing database user who joins that role. The statement does not create either the role or the user.
Review source

column1: A WHERE predicate on a dynamically masked column evaluates the {{c1::original, unmasked values}}.
column2:
SQL Server evaluates the WHERE condition against stored values before masking the displayed result. A salary filter can therefore match a real salary even when SELECT displays 0. Masking is a display restriction, not a change to comparison values.
Review source

column1: To test DDM in Fabric SQL database, connect as {{c1::a different user without effective UNMASK}}, with SELECT access.
column2:
Use a separate connection for a user with SELECT but no UNMASK from any permission source. An administrator's connection can display original values and hide test failures. Fabric SQL database does not support EXECUTE AS USER for this test.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2022+, mask the year component with FUNCTION = '{{c1::datetime("Y")}}'.
column2:
datetime("Y") masks the year component of a date or time value. The uppercase Y selects the year. Unlike default(), this function targets a selected component rather than replacing the entire date.
Review source

column1: GRANT UNMASK TO DataAnalyst; grants UNMASK at {{c1::database scope}}.
column2:
Without an ON clause, this UNMASK grant applies at database scope. It allows original masked values only where DataAnalyst also has SELECT. For narrower exposure, use a supported schema, table, or column scope.
Review source
